topic: AI Productivity Paradox: Why Your Team Feels Faster But Ships Less

key_points: Defines the paradox as the gap between perceived AI speed and measured software delivery.
Uses METR's early-2025 RCT as the anchor statistic: experienced open-source developers took 19% longer with AI while believing they were faster.
Frames missing institutional context as the main cause of plausible-but-wrong AI output and downstream rework.
Positions context systems as the practical fix for making AI useful inside mature codebases.
Argues that AI changes the meaning of productivity measurement because output volume is a weak proxy for value.
Warns that mature systems need reliability and business outcomes more than more generated code.
Reframes success as shipping less code when that code carries more value and lower operational risk.
Names the team-level problem as a fragmentation tax: faster individuals still lose value to unclear goals, duplicated work, and poor coordination.
Estimates the Fortune 500 cost of AI-related fragmentation at $161 billion annually.
Recommends treating AI as part of team workflows rather than a personal productivity hack.
Separates faster coding from faster software delivery.
Highlights that AI can increase code production while organizational delivery metrics remain flat.
Points to build, test, review, and delivery-system bottlenecks as the places where AI gains disappear.
Reports telemetry from more than 10,000 developers across 1,255 teams.
Finds AI-assisted developers produce more code, complete more tasks, and parallelize more work.
Finds the company-level productivity signal evaporates as bigger, buggier work shifts bottlenecks into review and quality control.

stats.fact: METR's early-2025 randomized controlled trial found experienced open-source developers took 19% longer with AI tools; METR later cautioned that these historical results no longer fully reflect early-2026 AI capabilities.

METR's February 2026 update says measuring AI productivity has become harder because many developers avoid tasks where AI is disallowed; raw late-2025 estimates showed possible speedups, but METR called the signal unreliable due to selection effects.
Glean's Work AI Index 2026 reports workers spend 6.4 hours per week botsitting AI, or 37% of their AI time, on context loading, checking, debugging, rerunning prompts, and cleanup.
Glean reports 87% of digital workers use AI, but only 13% say AI has significantly improved company performance.
Atlassian estimates AI-related team fragmentation costs the Fortune 500 $161 billion per year when individual AI speed does not translate into coordinated outcomes.
Deloitte's 2026 State of AI in the Enterprise says AI is delivering efficiency and productivity, but only 34% of leaders are truly reimagining the business.
McKinsey's 2025 global AI survey reports 88% of organizations use AI in at least one business function, but only about one-third have begun scaling AI programs enterprise-wide.
McKinsey finds high-performing AI organizations are nearly three times as likely as others to have fundamentally redesigned individual workflows, making workflow redesign a key predictor of value.
Faros reports AI-assisted engineering increases visible activity but loses correlation with key performance metrics at company level as review, quality, and coordination bottlenecks grow.

angles: The paradox is not that AI is useless; it is that teams are measuring the wrong layer of work.
AI makes the first draft faster and the system of delivery more sensitive to weak review, missing context, and unclear ownership.
The new bottleneck is not typing code; it is deciding, validating, integrating, and operating code.
Botsitting is the hidden labor line item that turns reported time savings into organizational drag.
The most useful 2026 stance is post-hype but not anti-AI: keep AI, change the workflow around it.
Teams should measure cycle time to production, escaped defects, review load, incident rate, rework, and business outcomes rather than prompts used, PRs opened, or lines generated.
The fix is a delivery operating system: narrower work units, better context, AI-ready acceptance criteria, review budgets, quality gates, and fewer handoffs.
